q: Burgundy's 1936 hierarchy did not appear from nothing. Trace it back: who ranked the climats, when, and how did that ranking become law?
accept: jules lavalle 1855 ranked the climats, beaune committee of agriculture 1861, carried into the 1936 decrees
lavalle's 1855 book with tete de cuvee and first second third cuvee became the 1861 classification and then the aoc decrees
dr lavalle 1855 then the beaune agricultural committee in 1861, formalised by inao from 1936
the 1855 lavalle ranking of vineyards, official in 1861, converted to grand cru premier cru and village
ans: Dr Jules Lavalle's Histoire et Statistique de la Vigne et des Grands Vins de la Côte-d'Or, published in 1855, mapped the Côte and ranked its climats — Tête de Cuvée at the summit, then Première, Deuxième and Troisième Cuvée. The Beaune Committee of Agriculture took that work and issued an official classification in 1861 in three classes. When the INAO drew up the appellation decrees from 1936, those rankings were carried over almost wholesale into grand cru, premier cru and village. That inheritance explains two things: Burgundy classifies land rather than estates, and the hierarchy has barely moved since — La Grande Rue's promotion in 1992 and Pouilly-Fuissé's premiers crus in 2020 being the rare movements.
exp: 1855 is the same year as Bordeaux's classification, and the comparison is the whole point: Lavalle ranked pieces of ground by observed quality, while Bordeaux's brokers ranked châteaux by achieved price. Everything that follows — Burgundy's fragmentation, its indifference to brands, Bordeaux's estate culture — descends from that difference. The villages had already begun trading on their best sites by then, Gevrey having annexed Chambertin's name in 1847.

q: Your BTG Champagne costs $54; the room's ceiling for a glass is $28. Solve it three ways.
accept: coravin preservation smaller pour alternative producer half bottle
5 pours 10.80 cost 38 percent negotiate post-off feature crémant
ans: $54 ÷ 5 pours = $10.80 → 38.6% at $28. Three ways out: (a) tighten to a 4-oz pour (6 pours ≈ $9.00 → 32%) with Coravin or inert gas so nothing is lost to waste; (b) negotiate a post-off or list it by the half-bottle; (c) substitute a grower Champagne or crémant at target cost — or knowingly carry it as a loss-leader luxury
exp: Master business questions want options with trade-offs, not one right number.

q: Contribution margin versus pour cost — why can a 45% cost bottle beat a 25% one?
accept: higher dollar margin on expensive bottle
dollars in the till
dollars in the till instead of percentage
more gross margin dollars
dollars in the till not percentage
ans: A $200 bottle at 45% cost yields $110 gross; a $40 bottle at 25% yields $30. Percentages don't pay invoices — dollars do
exp: The single most important number in progressive markup's defense.

q: Your wine cost is 34% against a 28% target. Give three levers in order of speed.
accept: reprice btg features renegotiate purchasing menu engineering staff training
price mix purchasing
ans: Reprice the fastest-moving BTG and features (immediate), shift the sales mix through staff training and placement (weeks), renegotiate purchasing and post-offs (next cycle)
exp: Order the levers by how quickly they move the number.

q: Name the four categories of unlawful trade practice under the Federal Alcohol Administration Act and explain what each prohibits.
accept: exclusive outlet tied house commercial bribery and consignment sales
the four are exclusive outlet tied house bribery and the consignment sale ban
tied house exclusive outlet commercial bribery plus consignment sales
ans: Exclusive outlet: a supplier may not require a retailer to purchase its products to the exclusion of competitors. Tied house: an industry member may not induce a retailer to buy by furnishing a thing of value — free goods, equipment, signage beyond limits, paying the retailer's expenses, or acquiring an interest in the licence or the premises. Commercial bribery: no payments or gifts to a retailer's officers or employees to secure preference over a competitor. Consignment sales: no sales on consignment, conditional sale, sale-or-return, or with the privilege of return, so a supplier cannot park stock on a retailer's shelf at no risk. The provisions sit at 27 USC 205 and 27 CFR Parts 6, 8, 10 and 11, are enforced by the TTB, and turn in practice on whether the conduct excludes competitors from the market. Every state overlays its own rules, often stricter — some restrict sampling, travel, or how a supplier may host a buyer.
exp: Consignment is the one buyers forget: you cannot take stock you pay for only once it sells, and 'return it if it doesn't move' is not a favour a rep may lawfully grant. Knowing the four names lets you decline an offer on the rules rather than by accusing anyone of anything.
